analysis.one_liner: Bans insurers and federal health programs from requiring prior approval before covering care.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would bar health plans from using prior authorization and other utilization-management tools, sits without a committee hearing or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop health insurance plans, including Medicare, Medicaid, and other federal health programs, from requiring prior authorization, step therapy (trying cheaper drugs first), or medical necessity reviews before covering a doctor-ordered item or service. In plain terms, if your doctor orders it and your plan covers it, the plan would have to pay without a second gatekeeping review. It would take effect for plan years starting on or after January 1, 2026. The bill was introduced by one House member with no cosponsors and referred to two committees, where it has seen no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients whose care has been delayed, reduced, or denied by insurer review processes. That includes people in employer plans, individual market plans, Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, and federal employees' plans. Doctors and hospitals also benefit from spending less time fighting insurer reviews and from fewer overturned treatment decisions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients facing coverage denials and delays

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits group health plans and health insurers from imposing any prior authorization requirement, utilization management technique (including step therapy or fail-first protocols), or medical necessity review on any covered item or service [S3][S2].
Applies the same prohibition to federal health care programs, including Medicaid as administered by states and the federal employees' health program, beginning January 1, 2026 [S3].
For patients, this means a doctor's decision to order a scan, drug, or procedure would be covered without waiting for insurer sign-off, eliminating a common source of delayed or denied care [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, who would lose their main tools for limiting spending on care, and policyholders to the extent insurers raise premiums or reduce benefits to make up the difference. Federal and state governments could also see higher costs for Medicare, Medicaid, and other public programs if utilization rises once reviews are banned.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers, taxpayers, and premium payers

drawbacks.text: The bill bans all utilization management with no exceptions, removing insurers' ability to steer patients to lower-cost equivalent treatments, which could raise premiums and government program costs [S2][S3].

Insurers would bear higher payouts on covered services and could respond by raising premiums, raising deductibles and copays, or dropping coverage of discretionary services, shifting costs back onto patients [S3].

Unlike narrower reform proposals that would standardize and speed up prior authorization, this bill eliminates the process entirely rather than fixing it, an all-or-nothing approach that even allies of utilization-management reform might find too broad.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Patients would gain real, immediate relief from a well-documented problem: care denied or delayed by insurer paperwork. But the bill is blunt. Utilization management does sometimes catch inappropriate or wasteful care, and an outright ban gives insurers no way to manage costs except raising premiums or shifting costs to patients through deductibles. A narrower bill targeting abusive denials would capture much of the benefit with less risk. As written, patients likely gain at first, but some of that gain could be clawed back through higher premiums and government program costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees, which have taken no action on it since; with no cosponsors and no hearing, it has gone nowhere.

narrative.text: Rep. Jefferson Van Drew introduced the bill in the House on January 22, 2025 [S1][S5].
The same day, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Oversight and Government Reform Committee; no markup, hearing, or vote has followed [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, who keep their prior authorization and utilization-management tools and the spending control they provide, since the bill has not advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers keep their denial tools

for.name: Rep. Jefferson Van Drew
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and offered it for consideration.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Brett Guthrie (R)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and has not scheduled any markup, hearing, or floor consideration of the bill.

against.name: House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
against.what_they_did: Received a split referral and has taken no action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and the bill has no cosponsors, so its partisan support cannot be measured; it was sponsored by a single Republican and referred to committees controlled by his own party.

industries.industry: Health insurers and Medicare Advantage plans
industries.note: The bill strips insurers of prior authorization, step therapy, and medical necessity reviews, the mechanisms they use to hold down payouts on care. Insurers have opposed broad bans on these tools; if they lose them, expect higher premiums or shifted costs rather than absorbed losses.

industries.industry: Doctors, hospitals, and other health care providers
industries.note: Providers spend substantial staff time seeking insurer approvals and appealing denials; banning reviews removes that burden and removes insurer overrides of doctors' treatment decisions.

industries.industry: State Medicaid programs and federal program administrators
industries.note: States and federal agencies would lose the ability to require prior authorization in Medicaid and other public programs, which many states use to manage prescription drug spending. Federal and state budgets could face higher costs if utilization rises.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no committee action since the January 2025 referral, and a double committee assignment, the bill is effectively stalled. Unless it gains cosponsors and a committee hearing, the usual path for a bill at this stage is to sit until the Congress ends without a vote. Broader prior-authorization reform, if it moves, is more likely to come through narrower standardization measures than through this outright ban.
